title: Cascade, Inheritance, and Specificity
summary: Predict which declaration wins by reasoning about inheritance, selector specificity, and source order instead of adding increasingly complicated selectors.

quizDraft.title: Recognize inheritance
quizDraft.prompt: Which property commonly inherits from body to text descendants?
quizDraft.hint: Compare the child element with its surrounding element and ask whether the child has its own declaration for that property.

help.concept: Some CSS properties can flow from a surrounding element to nested content when the nested element does not set its own value.
help.hint_1: Look for the value the nested element would receive without adding another declaration to it.
help.hint_2: Choose the explanation based on the relationship between the surrounding rule and the nested element's computed style.

quizDraft.title: Reason about specificity and source order
quizDraft.prompt: Which statements about the cascade in this portfolio are correct? Select all that apply.
quizDraft.hint: Separate two ideas: how selector specificity ranks competing rules, and what happens when that ranking is tied.

help.concept: The cascade resolves direct declarations using importance, specificity, and then source order; inheritance fills gaps.
help.hint_1: A class selector outranks a type selector when both target the same element.
help.hint_2: Equal-specificity ties are resolved by the later matching declaration, while direct child declarations beat inherited values.

options: A class selector such as .intro is more specific than a plain p type selector.
When two matching selectors have equal specificity, the later declaration can win by source order.
An inherited color always overrides a color declared directly on the child element.
The first of two identical nav a selectors always wins because it appears first.

quizDraft.title: Complete the tie rule
quizDraft.prompt: Choose what breaks a tie when two matching selectors have equal specificity.
quizDraft.hint: Assume both rules have equal selector strength and target the same property. Focus on their position in the stylesheet.

help.concept: When competing declarations otherwise have equal priority, their placement in the stylesheet can break the tie.
help.hint_1: Compare which competing declaration appears after the other one.
help.hint_2: Choose the word that describes the declaration that comes after its equal-priority competitor.

quizDraft.title: Compare selector strength
quizDraft.prompt: Complete the statement about a class selector and a plain element selector.
quizDraft.hint: Compare a selector written with a dot-prefixed name against one written only as an HTML element name.

help.concept: Different selector forms contribute different amounts of specificity when they compete for the same property.
help.hint_1: A dot-prefixed selector has greater selector strength than a bare element-name selector.
help.hint_2: Choose the category used for a bare element-name selector such as `p`.

quizDraft.title: Use inheritance while separating the page chrome
quizDraft.prompt:
## CSS task

The typography is taking shape, but the central content and the repeated header/footer chrome still lack a clear relationship. Inheritance can establish a main text `color`, while a grouped selector can give repeated page chrome a shared surface and foreground without duplicating rules. Keep the cumulative stylesheet. Add `main { color: #334155; }`. Then add one grouped `header, footer` rule with `background-color: #e2e8f0;` and `color: #0f172a;`. Preview more than one page: nested main content should inherit predictably, and the header/footer should read as a distinct light-gray frame around the page.

### File to edit

`styles.css`

### Check your work

Keep the site's existing cumulative work, make the requested change, then compare the **Preview** with the **Expected result** before moving on.
quizDraft.hint: Keep the existing paragraph rule so you can observe where inheritance is overridden; share the chrome declarations between header and footer.

help.concept: Inheritance can establish a main text `color`, while a grouped selector can give repeated page chrome a shared surface and foreground without duplicating rules.
help.hint_1: Keep the existing paragraph rule so you can observe where inheritance is overridden; share the chrome declarations between header and footer.
help.hint_2: Preview more than one page: nested main content should inherit predictably, and the header/footer should read as a distinct light-gray frame around the page.

quizDraft.title: Resolve the site's shared text hierarchy with specificity
quizDraft.prompt:
## CSS task

Ordinary paragraphs, the Home intro, navigation, and section headings still need a clearer hierarchy. Specificity and relationship selectors let broad defaults coexist with stronger targeted roles instead of forcing page-specific markup. Set the existing `p` `color` to `#475569`, then set `.intro` to `color: #0f766e;`. Also strengthen the existing `nav a` styling with `font-weight: 600;` and `text-decoration: none;`, and add `main h2 { color: #0f766e; }`. Check Home plus another page: ordinary paragraphs should be muted, the intro should stay teal, nav links should feel stronger and cleaner, and main h2 headings should carry the accent.

### File to edit

`styles.css`

### Check your work

Keep the site's existing cumulative work, make the requested change, then compare the **Preview** with the **Expected result** before moving on.
quizDraft.hint: Keep the competing broad and targeted rules so the cascade has something meaningful to resolve.

help.concept: Specificity and relationship selectors let broad defaults coexist with stronger targeted roles instead of forcing page-specific markup.
help.hint_1: Keep the competing broad and targeted rules so the cascade has something meaningful to resolve.
help.hint_2: Check Home plus another page: ordinary paragraphs should be muted, the intro should stay teal, nav links should feel stronger and cleaner, and main h2 headings should carry the accent.

quizDraft.title: Finish the Module 1 cascade and typography checkpoint
quizDraft.prompt:
## CSS task

The final Module 1 pass needs to demonstrate source order while also tightening the remaining small typography roles. Equal-specificity rules make source order visible, and targeted descendant/class rules finish the hierarchy without changing the HTML. Add two equal-specificity `nav a` rules in order: first `color: #0f172a;`, then `color: #0f766e;`. Then add `header p { color: #475569; }` and refine `.intro` with `font-weight: 700;`. Preview the finished checkpoint: nav links should end teal because the later equal-specificity rule wins, header copy should be muted, and the Home intro should have the strongest emphasis.

### File to edit

`styles.css`

### Check your work

Keep the site's existing cumulative work, make the requested change, then compare the **Preview** with the **Expected result** before moving on.
quizDraft.hint: Use the same nav selector twice in the requested order, then refine the existing header paragraph and intro hooks.

help.concept: Equal-specificity rules make source order visible, and targeted descendant/class rules finish the hierarchy without changing the HTML.
help.hint_1: Use the same nav selector twice in the requested order, then refine the existing header paragraph and intro hooks.
help.hint_2: Preview the finished checkpoint: nav links should end teal because the later equal-specificity rule wins, header copy should be muted, and the Home intro should have the strongest emphasis.
